title: Analyse and respond to a variety of literary texts

lessons.title: Analysing a literary text
lessons.html:
Going beyond the story

To analyse a literary text means to take it apart to see how it works: how the writer builds characters, creates a mood, structures the plot and uses language to carry a message. Analysis moves beyond what happens to how and why.

The questions an analyst asks

  • Purpose: Is the text meant to entertain, persuade, protest, celebrate, teach or remember?
  • Audience: Who was it written for? A children's folk tale and a protest poem have different audiences.
  • Context: When and where was it written? South African texts from the apartheid years often deal with land, forced removals, labour and resistance; later texts often explore identity, change and reconciliation.
  • Point of view: Is it told in the first person (I) or third person (he, she, they)? How does this shape what we know?
  • Structure: How is the text organised? Does a story use flashbacks? Does a poem have stanzas that move from despair to hope?

Genres and their features

GenreFeatures to analyse
Short story / novelPlot structure, conflict, character development, setting, narrator
PoetryImagery, sound devices, rhythm, line breaks, tone
DramaDialogue, stage directions, dramatic tension, conflict between characters
Oral forms (izibongo, folk tales, songs)Repetition, call and response, praise names, performance

Plot structure

Many stories follow a pattern: exposition (introduction), rising action (complications), climax (turning point), falling action and resolution. Identifying the climax often reveals the central conflict and theme.

Before the next lesson, choose a short South African text and note its purpose, audience and point of view.

lessons.title: Literary devices and their effects
lessons.html:
The writer's toolbox

Naming a device is only the first step. Good analysis explains the effect of the device on the reader and how it supports the theme.

Common devices

  • Imagery: words that appeal to the senses. The cracked earth, the smell of rain that never came. Effect: makes drought vivid and painful.
  • Metaphor and simile: comparisons that create new meaning.
  • Symbolism: an object carrying a bigger idea, such as a fence representing division or the land representing identity and belonging.
  • Irony: a contrast between what is expected and what happens, or between what is said and meant. A character called Lucky who loses everything is ironic.
  • Foreshadowing: hints about what will happen later, building suspense.
  • Repetition and refrain: emphasises an idea, common in poetry and song.
  • Alliteration and onomatopoeia: sound effects, such as the drip, drip, drip of a tap.
  • Contrast: placing opposites together, such as a rich farmhouse and a poor worker's hut, to highlight inequality.

Analysing character

Consider how a character is revealed (actions, speech, others' reactions, narrator's comments), what motivates them, whether they change, and what they represent. A minor character may be a foil, showing up the qualities of the main character by contrast.

Writing an analytical paragraph

  1. Point: make a clear statement. The writer uses the image of the empty dam to show the family's hopelessness.
  2. Evidence: quote briefly from the text.
  3. Explanation: explain how the evidence supports your point and its effect on the reader.
  4. Link: connect back to the theme or question.

lessons.title: Responding critically and creatively
lessons.html:
Making your own response

Critical response

A critical response evaluates the text. Ask:

  • Does the text succeed in its purpose? Why or why not?
  • Are the characters believable?
  • Whose voices are heard and whose are missing? For example, does a farm story give the farm workers a voice, or only the owner?
  • Do you agree with the values or message of the text?
  • How does it compare with another text on a similar theme?

Support your judgement with evidence. Saying I did not like it is an opinion; saying the ending felt unconvincing because the conflict over the land was resolved in a single page without explanation is a critical response.

Creative response

You can also respond by creating:

  • A diary entry written by a character
  • A letter from one character to another
  • A new ending or a scene from a different point of view
  • A poem in response to the original
  • A short dramatised reading for the team

Creative responses show that you understand the characters and themes well enough to work with them.

Discussion

Literary texts are good for group discussion. Listen actively, build on others' points, disagree respectfully and give reasons. These are the same skills a supervisor uses in team meetings.

Relating texts to life and work

Texts about drought, land, migrant labour, family or community can help us reflect on our own experience on farms and in rural communities. Analysing how a writer handles conflict can also improve how we understand conflict at work.

Key points

  • Analysis asks how and why a text works, considering purpose, audience, context and structure.
  • Explain the effect of literary devices, not just their names.
  • Use point, evidence, explanation and link in analytical paragraphs.
  • Critical responses evaluate the text with evidence; creative responses reimagine it.
  • Ask whose voices are heard and whose are missing.
